111.event_title: Henry Dunant and the women of Castiglione after Solferino
111.place: Solferino and Castiglione delle Stiviere, Lombardy, Italy
111.event: Swiss businessman Henry Dunant arrived near the northern Italian town of Solferino in time to witness the aftermath of the battle of 24 June 1859 between the French and Piedmontese-Sardinian armies and the Austrian army. In nearby Castiglione delle Stiviere he joined local people caring for the wounded in the town's main church, which sheltered more than 500 men, and the town's women tended French, Italian and Austrian soldiers without distinction. Dunant's book A Memory of Solferino (1862) led to the founding of the Red Cross movement and to the first Geneva Convention, signed in 1864.
111.explanation: Care given equally to allies and enemies on a battlefield became the founding principle of impartial humanitarian aid.
111.tie_back: The kural calls it true fitness to deal rightly with enemies, strangers and friends alike; Dunant and the women of Castiglione treated soldiers of every army the same.
111._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of even-handed treatment of enemies, strangers and friends, applied to the care of the wounded.

112.event_title: Ernst Abbe creates the Carl Zeiss Foundation
112.event: Physicist Ernst Abbe, who became head of the Zeiss optical works after Carl Zeiss's death in 1888, was concerned that future owners might enrich themselves at the expense of the companies and their employees. In 1889 he set up and endowed the Carl Zeiss Foundation, which became sole owner of the Zeiss works in 1891, and his 1896 foundation statute gave employees rights such as profit-sharing, paid holidays, sick pay and pensions, with an eight-hour day introduced at Zeiss in 1900. The ZEISS company credits Abbe with a decisive role in the continued existence of ZEISS and SCHOTT, both of which still operate today.
112.explanation: Abbe chose to build fairness to workers into the ownership of the firm itself, so that it could not easily be undone by later owners.
112.tie_back: The kural says the prosperity of the just does not crumble but supports those who come after; Abbe's fairly organised enterprise has outlasted him by more than a century.
112._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for just wealth that endures for posterity, though the kural has a person's descendants in mind and the firm's long survival also owes much to other factors.

113.event_title: Eugenio Monti lends his bolt to his rivals
113.place: Igls, near Innsbruck, Austria (Winter Olympic Games)
113.event: During the two-man bobsleigh competition at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Olympics, a bolt on the sled of British rivals Tony Nash and Robin Dixon broke, threatening to put them out of the event. Italy's Eugenio Monti, one of the world's leading drivers, gave them a replacement bolt from his own equipment, and Nash and Dixon went on to win the Olympic title. Monti also had his team help repair the sled of the Canadian four-man crew, who won that event, and the International Olympic Committee later honoured him with its first Pierre de Coubertin fair-play award.
113.explanation: Monti could have gained a medal simply by staying silent, but he refused to profit from a rival's misfortune.
113.tie_back: The kural says any gain that comes from abandoning fairness should be given up at once; Monti gave up a likely advantage on the spot rather than win by his rivals' accident.
113._accuracy_note: A strong fit for renouncing an unfair advantage immediately, though the advantage came from chance rather than from any wrong done by Monti.

114.event_title: Justice Harlan's lone dissent in Plessy v. Ferguson
114.place: Supreme Court of the United States, Washington, D.C., United States
114.event: In Plessy v. Ferguson the US Supreme Court, by a vote of 7 to 1, upheld a state law providing for racial segregation and established the separate but equal doctrine. Justice John Marshall Harlan was the lone dissenter, arguing that the Constitution recognised no superior or ruling class among citizens and warning that the decision would plant the seeds of race hatred in state law. In 1954, in Brown v. Board of Education and related cases, the Court repudiated the separate but equal doctrine, and Britannica notes that in the twentieth century the Court vindicated many of the positions Harlan had taken in dissent.
114.explanation: Harlan was outvoted in his lifetime, but the judgment that survived him was his, while the majority's ruling is now remembered as a grave injustice.
114.tie_back: The kural says whether a person was just or unjust is revealed by what remains after them; history's verdict on Plessy showed who had judged fairly.
114._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the reputation reading of the kural; it does not illustrate the older reading about descendants.

115.event_title: Justice H. R. Khanna's dissent in ADM Jabalpur
115.place: Supreme Court of India, New Delhi, India
115.event: During the national Emergency of 1975-77, the Supreme Court of India ruled 4 to 1 in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla that detained citizens could not approach the courts to enforce their right to life and liberty while the Emergency lasted. Justice H. R. Khanna, next in line by seniority to become Chief Justice, was the lone dissenter, holding that life and liberty could not be at the mercy of the executive; he later wrote that before the judgment he had told his sister it would cost him the Chief Justiceship. In January 1977 a junior judge, M. H. Beg, was appointed Chief Justice instead, and Khanna resigned the same day; in 2017 a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court overruled the majority judgment.
115.explanation: Khanna knowingly gave up the highest judicial office in India rather than bend his reading of the law to the pressure of the moment.
115.tie_back: The kural says loss and gain will come, and the ornament of the noble is a heart that does not bend in either; Khanna accepted the loss and did not bend.
115._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of steadfast impartiality in the face of foreseen personal loss.

116.event_title: Former Prime Minister Tanaka and the Lockheed bribery scandal
116.event: Tanaka Kakuei, prime minister of Japan from 1972 to 1974, was accused of having accepted, while in office, the equivalent of about 2 million US dollars from the American aircraft maker Lockheed to influence All Nippon Airways to buy Lockheed airliners. He was arrested on 27 July 1976, and in 1983 the Tokyo District Court found him guilty and sentenced him to four years in prison and a fine of 500 million yen. He remained free while appealing, suffered a serious stroke in 1985 after which his power and influence waned, and died in 1993 before the appeal was decided.
116.explanation: A leader at the height of power who turned public office toward private gain saw his reputation and influence destroyed, and the case became a lasting symbol of political corruption in Japan.
116.tie_back: The kural warns that when the heart turns from fairness to wrongdoing, ruin is near; Tanaka's fall followed from a decision to sell the influence of his office.
116._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: the kural describes an inner warning sign, while the record shows only the outward consequences, which unfolded slowly over many years.

117.event_title: Sir Walter Scott chooses to repay his creditors
117.place: Edinburgh and Abbotsford, Scotland, United Kingdom
117.event: In January 1826 the collapse of Scott's publisher, Archibald Constable and Co., brought down the Ballantyne printing firm in which Scott was a partner, leaving him liable for debts of about 121,000 pounds. Rather than take trade bankruptcy, which would have let him pay creditors only a fraction of what they were owed, he placed his entire literary income in a trust for his creditors, sold his Edinburgh house and wrote intensively for the rest of his life. The creditors accepted, partly from reluctance to ruin a man regarded as a national treasure whose misfortune had aroused great public sympathy, and the debt was finally cleared after his death through the sale of his copyrights.
117.explanation: Scott chose poverty and years of overwork over an easier legal escape that would have shortchanged the people he owed, and his public standing survived the financial collapse.
117.tie_back: The kural says the world does not count it a downfall when one who holds to fairness becomes poor; Scott's ruin brought him sympathy rather than disgrace.
117._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for honourable poverty; Scott's own risky business dealings helped cause the crash, so his fairness lay in the response rather than the cause.

118.event_title: Athens chooses jurors by allotment machine
118.date: 4th century BCE (procedure described); surviving machines mid-2nd century BCE
118.event: Classical Athens chose many officials and jurors by lot rather than by election. The Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians gives a detailed account of how jurors for the courts were allotted, and stone allotment machines called kleroteria, found in and around the Athenian Agora, confirm that picture: citizens' bronze tickets were inserted into rows of slots, and an attached mechanical device made the selection by chance. The surviving inscribed machines date to the mid-second century BCE.
118.explanation: The Athenians built the removal of favouritism into the procedure itself, so that the panel was settled by chance before any case was weighed.
118.tie_back: The kural compares the just to a balance that first sets itself level and then weighs; the allotment machine levelled the scale before judgment began.
118._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for the idea of being level before weighing, but it illustrates an institution rather than a single person's inner steadiness, and dating details remain debated by scholars.

119.event_title: The secret file at Alfred Dreyfus's court-martial
119.event: In autumn 1894 French intelligence found that a secret military document had been sent to the German military attache in Paris, and Captain Alfred Dreyfus, the only Jewish officer on the army General Staff, was arrested on the basis of handwriting analysis. At his court-martial the war ministry placed before the judges a file of secret, and in some cases forged, documents that his lawyer was not allowed to see, and he was convicted of treason. Evidence later pointed to another officer, Ferdinand Walsin-Esterhazy, and in July 1906 the verdict against Dreyfus was set aside and he was exonerated.
119.explanation: The trial had the outward form of military justice, but the outcome was driven by hidden evidence and, according to the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, by anti-Jewish prejudice.
119.tie_back: The kural says fair words count as fairness only when the heart is free of bias; the Dreyfus court-martial shows a correct-looking procedure corrupted by crooked intent within.
119._accuracy_note: A counter-example rather than a model: it shows what the kural warns against, a straight outward form concealing a bent inner judgment.

120.event_title: The first Fairtrade label, Max Havelaar
120.place: Netherlands, with coffee from Oaxaca, Mexico
120.event: Indigenous coffee farmers of the UCIRI cooperative in Oaxaca, Mexico, asked the Dutch development organisation Solidaridad for access to European markets on equitable terms. Rather than start its own coffee brand, Solidaridad created the Max Havelaar label, launched on 15 November 1988, which could be placed on coffee of any brand whose buyers paid the farmers a price above the market rate plus a premium. The first labelled coffee came from UCIRI and was sold through world shops and mainstream retailers across the Netherlands, and similar labels spread across Europe, leading in 1997 to the umbrella organisation Fairtrade International.
120.explanation: The scheme asked traders and shoppers to treat the farmers' interests as part of the bargain instead of simply paying the lowest possible price.
120.tie_back: The kural says true trade means guarding others' interests as one's own; Max Havelaar turned that principle into a working label for ordinary commerce.
120._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the kural's ethic of trade, applied through a certification system rather than by a single merchant.
